title: Six of Swords Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: Six of Swords upright: transition, moving on, calmer waters; reversed: stuck halfway. Love, work, advice and Waite's 1911 text. Ask your question.
h1: Six of Swords Tarot Card Meaning
image_alt: Six of Swords, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a ferryman poles a boat with six upright swords and two passengers, one hooded, toward a far shore.
capsule: The Six of Swords means transition and moving on: a quiet journey away from trouble toward calmer waters. Reversed, the crossing stalls halfway, or old worries come along. It is a kind card that favors slow progress over a quick fix. As a yes or no answer it is not clear yet, since the boat is still mid-crossing.

blocks.heading: What is on the Six of Swords card?
paragraphs: Six swords stand upright in a small boat while a ferryman pushes it across the water with a long pole. Waite describes "a ferryman carrying passengers in his punt to the further shore" (p. 242), and he adds that the course is smooth and the load light, so "the work is not beyond his strength" (p. 242).

On the 1909 card the ferryman stands at the back, seen from behind in an orange tunic. In front of him sit two passengers: a hooded figure wrapped in a yellow cloak and a smaller one in gray. Small waves ripple at the lower right, the water further out lies flat, and a low shore with trees waits ahead; VI is printed at the top.

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about the Six of Swords?
paragraphs: Waite keeps this card practical (p. 242): a trip by water, a route, an envoy or agent sent on an errand, an expedient that gets a thing done. Among his additional meanings Waite keeps one old fortune-telling line, "the voyage will be pleasant" (p. 291); Arcana Diary does not read it as a forecast about any trip. His reversed list turns to speaking out, with a declaration, a confession, something made public, and in one account a proposal of love (p. 242).
Reading the crossing as an inner one, leaving a hard time behind, is the modern meaning, not Waite's.

blocks.heading: What does the Six of Swords mean upright?
paragraphs: Moving on is the core of this card. A breakup, a move, a new job or simply the end of a draining stretch: something is being left behind, and the next place offers more peace than the last. The tone is quiet, not triumphant. You may still feel the loss while already sensing relief.

This transition is gradual. The crossing does not erase what happened; it puts distance between you and the hardest part, one push of the pole at a time. A literal journey fits too, especially by water, as in Waite's list (p. 242).
Which shore am I steering toward, and what can stay behind?

blocks.heading: What does the Six of Swords mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, the Six of Swords can describe being stuck halfway: ready to leave something, yet not moving. Resisting change is one reason; unfinished business is another, a talk not yet had or a matter still open on the old shore. Sometimes you do move, but you carry old worries into the new place.

Waite's reversed side is different, with declaration and confession, things said in the open (p. 242); the stalled-crossing reading is modern. The two can meet in one step: say plainly what still ties you to the past, and notice what loosens.

blocks.heading: What does the Six of Swords mean in love?
paragraphs: Distance from pain is the modern love meaning: leaving a hard relationship or a painful chapter and heading toward something calmer. Waite records one account that reads the reversed card as a proposal of love (p. 242).

Couples meet this card when they get through a rough patch side by side, or move to a new home together. Unattached, you may be letting an old heartbreak fall behind before looking ahead. Reversed, the past keeps pulling: a former bond that is hard to leave, or old hurt carried into something new.

blocks.heading: What does the Six of Swords mean for work and money?
paragraphs: A job change, a transfer, leaving a tense workplace for a steadier one: the boat here carries you to calmer ground, even when the move is sideways rather than up. Work travel fits as well.
Slow recovery is the money side of the crossing: getting out of debt or strain step by step, toward a steadier budget. Reversed, it can mean old money troubles following you into a new situation.

blocks.heading: What is the advice of the Six of Swords?
paragraphs: Pick one worry you keep carrying, write it on a scrap of paper and tear it up. Then turn your attention to the next small step on the far side, not to the shore you left.

blocks.heading: Is the Six of Swords a yes or no card?
The Six of Swords as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: A crossing under way is the picture of the Six of Swords: it stands for someone in the middle of a change, quiet, a little worn, moving away from a hard time. It can also be the helper who carries others across, steady and calm like the ferryman. The feeling side is relief mixed with sadness, a longing for peace after trouble, sometimes shared and sometimes leading apart. Reversed, the feelings are stuck: unresolved hurt, a pull toward what was, or not being ready to move on.

blocks.heading: The Six of Swords with other cards

pairs.text: A deliberate goodbye, then the slow crossing toward something new.
Hope after the crossing. Calm returns and the road ahead looks kinder.
Leaving a fight behind. Not every conflict has to be won before you go.
A trip with a purpose: looking ahead and setting out toward it.

blocks.heading: Six of Swords or Eight of Cups?
paragraphs: Waite's Eight of Cups shows "a man of dejected aspect" leaving his cups behind (p. 210); today it is read as walking away from what no longer satisfies. In the Eight of Cups the leaving is a choice, made on foot and alone. In the Six of Swords the move is already under way, someone else holds the pole, and the point is the calmer place ahead.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about the Six of Swords
paragraphs: What am I ready to leave on the old shore?
What do I hope to find on the other side?
Who or what keeps me moving when the crossing feels slow?

faq.q: Is the Six of Swords a good or bad card?
faq.a: Mostly good, though never loudly so. It marks a turn away from difficulty, so it often appears once the worst has passed. It is not a card of instant joy: it asks for patience while things settle. Reversed, it shows where you are holding on, which is useful to know.

faq.q: Does the Six of Swords mean travel?
faq.a: It can. Waite's first meaning is a journey by water (p. 242), and modern readers still see trips, moves and relocations in it. Often, though, the trip is an inner one: from a troubled period into a steadier one, without leaving town.

faq.q: Does the Six of Swords mean someone is moving on from me?
faq.a: Not as a statement about any person. Asked about feelings, its traditional meaning is a wish to put pain behind and find peace; that can mean parting, or getting through a hard stretch together. The card does not say which. What it can show is your own next step.

waite.quote: Journey by water, route, way, envoy, commissionary, expedient. Reversed: Declaration, confession, publicity; one account says that it is a proposal of love.
